what_it_does: Cloud providers rent out access to FPGAs — chips whose internal circuitry can be reprogrammed by the customer — but deliberately hide information about which physical machine a customer's workload is running on, to prevent attacks that exploit traces left by previous tenants (such as residual data in the chip's memory, or electromagnetic signals that leak information). PhasePrint is an attack that circumvents this hiding by creating a unique physical fingerprint for each FPGA chip. Every chip comes off the manufacturing line with tiny, unintentional variations in how fast its transistors switch, caused by imperfect uniformity in the silicon. The paper shows that by deliberately pushing the chip's circuits to their timing limits — for example by running self-oscillating loops that stress the fabric — an attacker can trigger timing faults (glitches where a signal arrives fractionally too late) and observe the exact pattern of which circuits fail first. Because that failure pattern is determined by the chip's physical manufacturing variations, it is unique to that chip and reproducible, functioning as a fingerprint. A tenant can collect this fingerprint, then re-rent until they get the same fingerprint, effectively pinpointing a specific physical machine despite the cloud vendor's anonymization.
